catalog_quote: [p.28, sec. 2.1.2.3] Stress is non-phonemic. The most pronounced stress occurs on the first syllable of words, except verbs where it may occur elsewhere. Unaffixed verb roots of tone Class I are stressed on the first syllable: pona 'to cut', waraa 'to touch', rumaa 'to portion out'. Affixation of tone Class I verbs causes stress to shift to final stem syllable. Tone Class I verb stems are stressed on the second syllable: ruba 'to throw away'. tone_statements.citation: Franklin, Karl J. 2011. The Kewa language revisited. GIALens 5(2): 1-27. Dallas: Graduate Institute of Applied Linguistics.
tone_statements.quote: Tone. Tone is phonemic in all dialects but is unwritten in the practical orthography— except in contrastive pairs that prove difficult to otherwise interpret in reading, such as áá ‘man’, àà ‘feet’ (WK); pú ‘liver’, pù ‘urine’; [...] He also distinguishes between tone melody (on phonological words) and tone proper (on syllables) and finds, as we did, two phonemic tones, High and Low.

tone_statements.citation: Franklin, Karl J. 2010. The word in Kewa. In Loren Billings & Nelleke Goudswaard (eds.), Piakandatu ami Dr. Howard P. McKaughan, 110-134. Manila: Linguistic Society of the Philippines and SIL Philippines.
tone_statements.quote: Although every nuclear V carries either a high or low tone, there are perceptual problems because both tones are realized in certain environments as mid. ... Generally clitics and suffixes do not carry their own inherent tones, but are stressed and follow the lead of the tone of the last syllable of the stem to which they are attached. ... Normally a primary stress occurs on the first syllable of any noun stem of less than four syllables and on the second syllable of any stem over four, except in cases of reduplication or compounds.
tone_statements.locator: p.116 (sec. 2 Phonological considerations) and p.117 (sec. 2.2 Tonal patterns in words)
tone_statements.summary: Every vowel nucleus carries high or low tone, both realised as mid in certain environments; suffixes and clitics copy the stem-final tone; falling pitch noted on one monosyllable; word stress stated.

sources.citation: Franklin, Karl J. 1969. A grammar and dialect study of Kewa, New Guinea. PhD thesis, Australian National University (Part 1 of 3, hdl.handle.net/1885/10802).
sources.quote: 'The perceptual or auditory height of a tone may be conditioned by stress placement (Cf. Kewa I:35). Disregarding levels above the phonemic word, a primary stress occurs on the first syllable of any noun stem of less than four syllables and on the second syllable of any stem over four. Any basic low tone which occurs on such stressed syllables will be heard as mid.' Preface (p.iii) confirms the grammar describes West Kewa (fieldwork from 1967) while earlier published materials were East Kewa.
sources.locator: thesis p.36 sec 2.31 'Tonal Variation' (p.47); image-only microfilm scan, read from page scan

sources.citation: Franklin, Karl J. 1975. Nasalisation in Kewa dialects. Kivung 8(1): 72-86.
sources.note: scanned full text (pp. 72-86) read: the paper is about phonemic vowel nasalisation and its historical sources (loss of a relic suffix *-ngV, *l > n, *nd > t, intervocalic nasal loss) across Kewa dialects; it says nothing about Kewa tone and examples carry no systematic tone marking. The only tone remarks concern other languages: Huli 2SG pronoun 'identical.. but with a low tone' (p. 80) and MacDonald's Dadibi observation that 'syllables with nasalised vowels are always low tone, except for 3rd singular pronouns' (p. 80-81).
